item.title: AI in IT Interviews: Evil or the New Normal?
item.description:
In past years, using neural networks in technical interviews was practically considered cheating. Today, the situation is changing. AI is increasingly becoming a developer's working tool, and some companies are experimenting with interview formats that allow candidates to use it. But if a developer solves a problem with the help of a neural network, how can we understand if they truly understand the solution? This article gathers opinions from heads of various technical departments at "Kryptonite" company, and also finds out the attitude towards AI in interviews from the head of recruitment. AI has transformed the hiring market. AI is increasingly used both in development and in job searching. According to the Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025, 84% of surveyed developers already use AI tools in the development process or plan to start. Among professional developers, 51% use them daily. AI is also used in employment. According to a Gartner study conducted at the end of 2024 among 3290 job seekers, 39% used such tools in their job search, including for resume preparation and completing assessment tasks. The Russian market shows a similar trend. In September 2026, "Avito Rabota" and "MTS Link" published the results of a survey of 10,000 people: 40% of respondents have used AI at least once to prepare for an interview. Among job seekers aged 18-24, the proportion who used AI was 65%, and among people over 55, it was 26%. Read more

item.title: How to Properly Choose Tasks for LLMs and Avoid Architectural Mistakes
item.description:
This article is for two categories of readers. The first are those who are starting to integrate LLMs into a working project. The demo is already working, the manager has seen the screenshots, and now it's time to turn it into a system that will survive contact with real users, real data, and a real budget. Here are the rules that help avoid redoing the architecture in two months. The second are those who are already deeply immersed in the topic. You understand how models work, follow releases, know how to get quality out of a prompt, and know the difference between one output mode and another. And that's precisely why you sometimes lose sight of a simple question: should the model even be involved in this part of the task? The ability to configure a model and the ability to determine its place in the system are different skills. The main idea of the text: LLMs are translators between human text and strict data structures, not the core of the system. Everything else follows from this rule. If you already disagree, you might not want to read further and should forgive the author for their subjective opinion. What the article will cover: Four signs of tasks where LLMs are truly appropriate. Six anti-patterns that most often break implementations. A principle for designing model responses that can be verified by code before use. Five analyzed examples of "LLM + program code" combinations: from secure database queries to multi-stage sum verification in contracts and control of RAG responses over a corporate knowledge base. A five-point checklist that can be attached to an architecture review. What the article will NOT cover: Comparisons of models, benchmarks, and framework reviews - all of this will become outdated faster than the text. Prompting techniques and recipes for "how to ask better." Analysis of transformer architecture, model training, and fine-tuning. A step-by-step guide to building a knowledge base search: choosing a storage, document slicing, selecting models for search. An exhaustive catalog of attacks and defense methods - the principle is shown here, not a full security reference. A ready-made library and code repository. About expectations: This is an engineering text, not a scientific publication. There are no proofs for every statement and no links to research. Some formulations are intentionally categorical: a rule that is remembered and applied during review is more useful than a precise but unused caveat. Examples are simplified to their essence. They show the principle, not industrial code: you will add timeouts, retries, and logging yourself, according to your stack. The rules describe a typical situation, not all possible ones. If you know a specific case where a recommendation doesn't work, it's likely true. This is not a reason to discard the rule, but a reason to know its boundaries. The goal of the text is simple: after reading it, you should be able to look at your system's architecture and say - this part we give to the model, this part we leave to the code, and here we need a validator - and clearly explain why.

item.title: The Fate of the Global IT Market
item.description:
The fate of the global IT market. Agree, everyone wants to know what awaits them in the future, and IT specialists are no exception. Everyone is currently concerned about the future of IT. Some say AI will replace everyone, some say AI will simply reduce the number of jobs, and some believe that AI will, on the contrary, increase the number of jobs in the future. In this article (and potentially a series of articles), I would like to determine with you, my dear Reader, the most likely outcome of events for the global IT hiring market. I suggest starting from the beginning, namely, defining concepts (as befits a good discussion, even if it is a remote one between us). 1. When will the future arrive? First, it would be good to determine the time frame whose fate we want to know. It is clear that taking values like twenty years does not make sense yet, as even the prospects for the next month are extremely unclear in the current situation, but looking for what will happen in a year would be too petty to release a series of remote discussions about it. I propose a compromise solution of 3-5 years, and leave all reflections on the more distant future without in-depth discussion, so as not to spread our forces too thin. 2. What do we consider the IT hiring market? Does it include product managers and similar specialists? Do we consider small companies? Do we take into account pure hands-off leads? My personal opinion (and I will be glad if you challenge it) is that we should include everything and anything that has at least a little to do with IT in this market. Include HR, managers, of course, the developers themselves, while also considering any company, even if it has only one first-year developer who occasionally paints buttons on a single CMS website. 3. item.title: SGNE-CC v2 Patch for DeepSeek-R1-1.5B (T=0): -87% Hangs, 2.7x Shorter Answers, and +11pp on MATH-500
item.description:
When greedily selecting tokens (T=0, no sampling or repetition penalty), the reasoning model DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B often gets stuck in infinite loops of re-checking its own solution within tags, hitting the 32,768 token limit. I ported the open-source norm-preserving weight edit SGNE-CC from the hybrid Qwen3.5-0.8B to this pure transformer without fine-tuning or inference code changes. To stop the self-looping within the weights, it was enough to rotate just 205 mlp.down_proj columns (0.0177% of parameters, 603KB patch), leaving attention layers, gates, and normalizations untouched. Gains in greedy mode (T=0): on MATH-500 accuracy increased from 65% to 76% (+11pp), on programming tasks MBPP from 53% to 68%, on logic BBH from 68% to 78%. Fewer hangs and tokens (across 5 datasets, 1,054 tasks): the share of unfinished reasoning dropped by 87%, and the average answer length decreased 2.7-fold (10.8k -> 4.0k tokens). With standard sampling (T=0.6): accuracy is not lost (73% vs 72%), residual hangs also decrease by 86%, and generation becomes a third shorter. Below the fold: localization of the self-copying loop in attention heads, the geometry of the patch, honest boundaries of the method (HumanEval, T=0.3), and links to the patch and 32K traces. Read more

item.title: AI Claude Solves Two Long-Standing Black Hole Physics Problems
item.description:
Anthropic's AI model Claude has reportedly solved two long-standing problems in theoretical physics related to black holes. The solutions, published in two preprints, could aid in the search for a quantum theory of gravity. The research began with an unusual experiment where Claude was tasked with identifying unsolved problems, proposing 22. Multiple instances of Claude then worked in parallel for six weeks, exchanging results and verifying calculations. For the first problem, calculations were performed in two independent ways. For the second, results were further verified using the Lean formal verification system. Both studies leverage the holographic duality principle, which suggests that some gravitational theories can be described by non-gravitational quantum theories on their boundaries. The first problem concerns the Hawking-Page transition, a 1983 phenomenon where a gas of particles in anti-de Sitter space transitions to a black hole state, akin to a phase transition. The AI confirmed this transition remains sharp even in the quantum regime where spacetime geometry is not well-defined. The second problem involved modular bootstrap, a method for testing the consistency of quantum gravity theories. Claude identified a pattern in numerical results, leading to an analytical derivation of a precise bound for a key characteristic, improving upon previous estimates.

item.title: 411 comments in a pull request and other tasks we've handed over to AI
item.description:
Hi, I'm Arina, a system analyst at YooMoney. AI has firmly entered our profession: it's used for gathering information, analyzing code, preparing technical documentation, and reviewing solutions. But how can we integrate it into our work without wasting time on endless edits and losing our own expertise? We've moved beyond prompt experiments and started building an automation system based on AI agents. They assist at various stages, from gathering context to updating documentation. The analyst still makes the decisions and is responsible for the outcome. In this article, I'll share my experience and practices of using AI agents in the daily tasks of a system analyst. The material will be primarily useful for colleagues in the profession: those who already use AI or are looking for scenarios for automation. Although we'll be discussing system analyst tasks, many of the described practices will also be useful for team leads and business analysts. I'll explain which tasks we delegate to agents, how we organize their work, and why it's sometimes better to ask AI to argue with you rather than invent a solution for you. Read on
